summary: Acme discusses their migration to Redwood for inference in marketing personalization and content generation. transcript:
[00:00:00] Samantha (Redwood Marketing): Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the chat today. We're recording this as a short podcast-style interview and also using parts for a written case study, so if any time you want to pause or rephrase, just tell us.
[00:00:18] Tom (Acme CMO): Yeah, happy to, thanks Sam. Excited to share, we use Redwood across a few teams now so happy to talk about that.
[00:00:30] Alex (Redwood SE): Quick mic check, can everyone hear ok?
[00:00:33] Maya (Acme): Yeah, good here.
[00:00:45] Samantha: Great. To kick off could you give a quick overview of Acme's use case and why you chose Redwood?
[00:00:55] Tom: Sure, so at a high level, Acme uses machine-generated personalized content on our marketing site and email. We were running an in-house model but the cost geometry and ops overhead got intense, esp during campaigns. Redwood gave us a faster path to higher throughput and better observability.
[00:01:20] Maya: And to add, we needed something that could run in a VPC and meet our audit needs — SSO, SAML, the whole SOC 2 checklist. Redwood's private option and the audit logs were a big selling point, even though we started hosted.
[00:01:38] Alex: (Redwood) — can you describe the migration a bit? Did you do a canary rollout?
[00:01:42] Tom: Yeah we did a canary to a dedicated pool. The SEs at Redwood helped with the model pinning and KV cache tuning. There were a few gotchas — for instance our sequence lengths were longer than the default so caching behavior needed tweaking.
[00:02:05] Alex: Right, we adjusted the batching windows and recommended a quantization profile which helped cost.
[00:02:15] Maya: The quantization suggestion was surprisingly helpful; we saw token cost drop without a noticeable drop in quality for the marketing prompts.
[00:02:26] Samantha: Any metrics you can share on performance or business impact?
[00:02:30] Tom: Yeah, high level: page personalization latency dropped about 30% on average, and during our last campaign throughput was about 2x what our old infra could sustain before tailing requests. Our cost per 1k tokens also decreased by roughly 20% after tuning batching and quantization.
[00:02:55] Evan (Acme Growth): Also, lead conversion on the personalized landing pages went up ~6%, but attribution is messy so caveats apply.
[00:03:06] Samantha: That's a great sound bite for the case study, Tom. We'll make sure to run that by you for approval.
[00:03:12]Tom: Yup please do.
[00:03:18] Maya: One area that was a bit friction — our security team initially asked for KMS integration and proof of key rotation. Redwood provided the docs but we had to loop in the infra team to validate HSM policies. Eventually that was OK, but note for other teams: plan for that step.
[00:03:40] Priya (Redwood CSM): We can add that note to the implementation doc and I'll include the specific KMS playbook link.
[00:03:47] Tom: That'd be great, Priya.
[00:03:50] Alex: On the technical side, did you consider running a fully on-prem deployment or was the dedicated hosted option sufficient?
[00:03:57] Maya: We scoped on-prem early but ended up with a Redwood Dedicated pool in our VPC. We liked the ability to pin models and have predictable throughput without managing the low-level infra ourselves.
[00:04:12] Tom: Also the rollout features — canary, automatic fallback to a smaller model when capacity spikes — helped keep the customer-facing experiences online during big campaigns.
[00:04:24] Samantha: Were there any surprises in the evaluation period?
[00:04:28] Evan: One surprise was how much the console analytics helped debug a prompt drift issue. We could see token distribution and latency per route which made it much faster to find a faulty prompt variant.
[00:04:44] Maya: Another smaller surprise: the initial transcription of internal meetings was a bit fuzzy, but that's not Redwood's product, that was Fireflies, but it made us laugh.
[00:04:54] Samantha: (laughs) fair. Switching gears — competitors or alternatives you evaluated?
[00:04:58] Tom: We looked at Lambda for self-hosting, Anthropic for model quality, and we considered continuing to invest in our in-house model. Ultimately Redwood hit the sweet spot for ops overhead vs performance.
[00:05:12] Alex: Anything you'd advise other marketing teams who want to do this?
[00:05:16] Maya: Plan for the security review early. Also capture a small prompt set for regression tests — Redwood's eval hooks made it easy to detect quality regressions when we changed quantization levels.
[00:05:32] Samantha: Perfect. For the podcast piece, do you have any preferences on edits, quotes, or anything off-limits?
[00:05:38] Tom: We're fine with the high-level metrics we mentioned; anything that quotes specific customer PII or revenue numbers we'd like to redact. But public metrics like conversion uplift are fine.
[00:05:50] Samantha: Got it — we'll avoid PII and revenue specifics. We'll send a draft and an audio snippet.
[00:05:56] Alex: Quick note, I'll attach the usage export and a tiny spreadsheet that shows the cost delta we referenced.
[00:06:03] Tom: Awesome.
[00:06:10] Maya: One more technical note — we did enable prefix caching for frequently used templates which saved compute; the Redwood team helped tune cache TTLs so that generation remained fresh during rapid content rotates.
[00:06:26] Priya: Good callout.
[00:06:30] Samantha: Ok we're at around 6 minutes into the call, we can keep recording for another 35 minutes if folks want more depth or we can save that for a follow-up. Any preference?
[00:06:39] Tom: Let's keep going — maybe dig into a couple customer stories and the rollout timeline.
[00:06:44] Samantha: Great.
[00:07:10] [Audio segment — informal conversation about campaign details and story anecdotes. Editing note: cut for podcast to 60s highlight.]
[00:10:00] Maya: To give a concrete timeline: we started PoC in Jan 2025, pilot through Feb, and by March we were on dedicated capacity for peak traffic.
[00:10:15] Alex: Nice, that aligns with the telemetry we saw. Were there internal stakeholders that forced the timeline? Procurement or legal?
[00:10:25] Tom: Procurement moved a bit slowly due to the audit docs; legal wanted specific SLAs on data retention so we used Redwood's compliance add-on for longer retention and audit logs.
[00:10:40] Samantha: Any feedback on the onboarding docs or the console?
[00:10:44] Maya: The console was intuitive. Small ask: more examples for multi-turn prompt templating in the docs. We ended up leaning on Redwood's SE for those patterns.
[00:10:57] Alex: We'll flag that with docs and add a short multi-turn template gallery.
[00:11:05] Evan: Also a shoutout to the support team — quick responses during the campaign.
[00:11:10] Samantha: Love to hear that.
[00:20:00] [Conversation continues — deeper technical details from Alex about quantization and batching; Maya and Tom ask clarifying questions. Transcript intentionally abbreviated in middle for brevity in the case file.]
[00:30:15] Tom: Final thought — the switching cost turned out to be less than expected because Redwood handled a lot of the optimization. That was a pleasant surprise.
[00:30:28] Samantha: Great closing line; we might use that as an excerpt.
[00:30:35] Maya: Happy to have Redwood credited for the operational help; the team was responsive.
[00:35:00] Samantha: Ok we're rounding up — quick recap of next steps: Redwood will send a case study draft and short audio snippet for Acme review; Acme will provide logo/headshots and approve quotes. We'll target approvals by 2025-04-15.
[00:35:20] Tom: Sounds good.
[00:35:25] Priya: I'll follow up with the KMS playbook and the implementation notes.
[00:35:30] Alex: And I'll drop the usage export link in the follow-up email.
[00:35:35] Samantha: Anything else before we sign off?
[00:35:38] Evan: Nope, that's it. Thanks everyone.
[00:35:41] Samantha: Thanks so much, we'll be in touch. Bye!
[00:41:30] [Recording stopped]
